## Variance reduction {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

Suppose

$$
\mu=\Ex[f(X)]=\Ex[g(X)],
\qquad X\sim\Unif[0,1]^d
$$

Both IID sample means are unbiased:

\begin{align*}
\hmu_{f,n}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(X_i),&
\hmu_{g,n}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}g(X_i)
\end{align*}

Their mean squared errors are their variances:

\begin{align*}
\var(\hmu_{f,n})&=\frac{\var\{f(X)\}}n,&
\var(\hmu_{g,n})&=\frac{\var\{g(X)\}}n
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
Deck 01 showed that accepting some bias can reduce MSE. Here both estimators
are unbiased, so an equivalent expectation is better when its
[integrand has smaller variance]{.alert}
:::

## The Keister example {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

Consider

$$
\mu=\int_{\reals^d}\cos(\norm{t})\exp(-\norm{t}^2)\,\dif t
$$

Let $x_j=\Phi(at_j)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF

Then $t_j=\Phi^{-1}(x_j)/a$ and

\begin{multline*}
\mu=\int_{[0,1]^d}\frac{(2\mpi)^{d/2}}{a^d}
\cos\!\left(\frac{\norm{\Phi^{-1}(x)}}a\right)\\
\times\exp\!\left[-\frac{2-a^2}{2a^2}\norm{\Phi^{-1}(x)}^2\right]\,\dif x,
\qquad a^2\le2
\end{multline*}

The parameter $a$ creates a [family of unbiased estimators]{.alert} with different variances

## Transforming an integral {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

To approximate $\mu=\int_{\mathcal T}g(t)\,\dif t$, choose an invertible map

$$
t=\psi(x),
\qquad \psi:\mathcal X\to\mathcal T
$$

Let $J(x;\psi)=\det\{\partial\psi_i/\partial x_j\}_{i,j=1}^d$

If $X$ has density $\varrho_X$, then

\begin{align*}
\mu
&=\int_{\mathcal X}g\{\psi(x)\}\abs{J(x;\psi)}\,\dif x\\
&=\Ex_{X\sim\varrho_X}\!\left[
\frac{g\{\psi(X)\}\abs{J(X;\psi)}}{\varrho_X(X)}
\right]
\end{align*}

For $X\sim\Unif[0,1]^d$, the density in the denominator is one

## Transforming a random variable {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

Let $\vZ$ have proposal density $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ and define
$\vX=T(\vZ)$ for an invertible map $T:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$

The densities satisfy

\begin{align*}
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)
&=\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}\{T^{-1}(\vx)\}
  \left|\det\nabla T^{-1}(\vx)\right|,\\
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\{T(\vz)\}
&=\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)}
{\left|\det\nabla T(\vz)\right|}
\end{align*}

Therefore

$$
\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[h(\vX)]
=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}[h\{T(\vZ)\}]
$$

[A change of variables in an integral]{.alert} and [a transformation of a random variable]{.alert} are the same mechanism viewed from opposite directions

## Transport makes importance weights constant {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

For any invertible map $T$,

\begin{align*}
\mu
&=\int h(\vx)\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)\,\dif \vx\\
&=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}\!\left[
h\{T(\vZ)\}
\underbrace{
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\{T(\vZ)\}
\left|\det\nabla T(\vZ)\right|}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vZ)}}_{W_T(\vZ)}
\right]
\end{align*}

- [Exact transport]{.alert}: choose $T$ so that $W_T(\vz)=1$ everywhere
- [Importance sampling]{.alert}: choose $T(\vz)=\vz$ and retain the varying
  weight $W_T(\vz)=\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vz)/
  \varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)$

::: {.key-point}
Transport absorbs the density correction into the map; importance sampling
carries the correction as a weight
:::

## Importance sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

Choose a proposal density $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ that is positive wherever
$h\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$ is nonzero:

\begin{align*}
\mu
&=\int h(x)\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)\,\dif x\\
&=\Ex_{Z\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}}\!\left[
h(Z)\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(Z)}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(Z)}
\right]
\end{align*}

The ratio $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}/\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ is the
[importance weight]{.alert}

For $Z_0,\ldots,Z_{n-1}\ \IIDsim\ \varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$,

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{IS},n}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h(Z_i)
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(Z_i)}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(Z_i)}
$$

---

### One integral, two estimators

Let

$$
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)=\exp(-x),
\qquad
\mu=\int_0^\infty x^2\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)\,\dif x=2,
\qquad
Z_i\ \IIDsim\ \Exp(1/2)
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
#### Transport

Move every proposal point using $T(z)=z/2$:

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{T},n}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}
\left(\frac{Z_i}{2}\right)^2
$$

The transformed points are equally weighted $\Exp(1)$ target samples
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
#### Importance sampling

Keep every proposal point and use

$$
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(z)}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)}
=2\exp(-z/2)
$$

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{IS},n}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2Z_i^2\exp(-Z_i/2)
$$
:::
:::

---

### Proposal choice depends on the integrand

For the same $Z\sim\Exp(1/2)$ proposal,

| Estimator contribution | Variance |
|:---|---:|
| Transport: $(Z/2)^2$ | $20$ |
| Importance sampling: $2Z^2\exp(-Z/2)$ | $188/81\approx2.32$ |

- The heavier-tailed proposal visits large $x$, where
  $x^2\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)$ is important
- The importance proposal is tailored to this $h(x)=x^2$
- Transport produces target samples that can be reused for any integrand
- A poor importance proposal can instead create extreme weights

::: {.key-point}
Transport primarily builds [reusable target samples]{.alert}; importance
sampling can instead tailor its proposal and weights to a
[particular integral]{.alert}
:::

## Brownian motion with drift {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="quant-finance"}

Positive option payoffs may be rare under a discretized Brownian path

Let $X\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mSigma)$ with $\Sigma_{jk}=\min(t_j,t_k)$ and
target density $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$

Use the proposal $\Norm(\va,\mSigma)$ with density
$\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ and

$$
\va=\theta(t_1,\ldots,t_d)^\mathsf T
$$

The likelihood ratio simplifies to

$$
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)}{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(x)}
=\exp\!\left(-\theta x_d+\frac{\theta^2t_d}{2}\right)
$$

- Drift makes positive payoffs more common
- Importance weights compensate to preserve the target expectation
- A good drift can [reduce estimator variance]{.alert}

## Choosing a transformation {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

- Variable transformation and importance sampling are intertwined
- The sampling density changes the variance of the sample mean
- Require
  - a finite Jacobian determinant
  - a proposal density that does not vanish where the integrand is nonzero
- Pilot samples can guide the choice of transformation or proposal

::: {.key-point}
Place more samples where the [magnitude of the integrand times the target density]{.alert} is large, without creating extreme weights
:::

- [Practical control-variate choices](#practical-control-variate-choices)

## Control variates {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

Let $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_m$ have known zero means

For any coefficients $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m$,

$$
\mu=\Ex[f(X)]
=\Ex\!\left[f(X)-\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j\eta_j(X)\right]
$$

The estimator

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{CV},n}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left[f(X_i)-\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j\eta_j(X_i)\right]
$$

is unbiased for fixed $\vbeta$

Choose $\vbeta$ to make

$$
\var\!\left[f(X)-\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j\eta_j(X)\right]
$$

as small as possible

## Choosing coefficients by least squares {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

Center the response and control values:

\begin{align*}
y_i&=f(x_i)-\bar f,&
H_{ij}&=\eta_j(x_i)-\bar\eta_j
\end{align*}

Then

$$
\hvbeta=\argmin_{\vb}\norm{\vy-\mH\vb}^2
$$

When $\mH^\mathsf T\mH$ is nonsingular,

$$
\hvbeta=(\mH^\mathsf T\mH)^{-1}\mH^\mathsf T\vy
$$

The residual is orthogonal to the column space of $\mH$, so least squares removes the component of $f$ explained by the controls

## Practical control-variate choices {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

- Good controls are inexpensive, have known means, and are strongly related to $f$
- More controls can reduce the sample size needed for a target accuracy
- Poor controls may increase computation without reducing variance
- For IID sampling, least squares targets variance reduction
- For low discrepancy sampling, choose coefficients to reduce [variation]{.alert}, not sampling variance

::: {.key-point}
A control variate turns [known expectations]{.alert} into information about an unknown expectation
:::

## Conditional Monte Carlo {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="prob-est"}

Recall

\begin{align*}
\Ex(Y)&=\Ex_Z\{\Ex(Y\mid Z)\},\\
\var(Y)&=\Ex_Z\{\var(Y\mid Z)\}+\var_Z\{\Ex(Y\mid Z)\}
\end{align*}

Therefore

$$
\var_Z\{\Ex(Y\mid Z)\}\le\var(Y)
$$

If $Y=f(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ and

$$
g(X_{2:d})=\Ex(Y\mid X_{2:d})
$$

is analytic, estimate $\mu$ by sampling $g(X_{2:d})$ instead of $Y$

[Analytically averaging over part of the randomness reduces variance]{.alert}

## Conditional density estimation {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="prob-est"}

Let $Y=f(X)$ with $X\sim\Unif[0,1]^d$

Suppose $f$ is increasing in $x_1$ and

$$
y=f(x_1,x_{2:d})iff x_1=g(y;x_{2:d})
$$

Then

\begin{align*}
F_{Y\mid X_{2:d}}(y\mid x_{2:d})
&=\Prob\{X_1\le g(y;x_{2:d})\}\\
&=g(y;x_{2:d}),\\
\varrho_Y(y)
&=\int_{[0,1]^{d-1}}\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}(y;x)\,\dif x
\end{align*}

Thus a density value becomes an [expectation of a conditional density]{.alert}

## Density of a sum of uniforms {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="practice"}

Let

$$
Y=\gamma_1X_1+\cdots+\gamma_dX_d,
\qquad X\sim\Unif[0,1]^d,
\qquad \gamma_j>0
$$

Solving for $x_1$ gives

$$
g(y;x_{2:d})=\frac{y-\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jx_j}{\gamma_1}
$$

when $\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jx_j\le y\le\gamma_1+\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jx_j$

Hence

$$
\varrho_Y(y)=\Ex\!\left[
\frac1{\gamma_1}\indic\!\left{
\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jX_j\le y\le
\gamma_1+\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jX_j
\right}\right]
$$

## Antithetic sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="sampling"}

If $T(X)$ has the same distribution as $X$, pair $f(X_i)$ with $f\{T(X_i)\}$:

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{Anti},n}
=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left[f(X_i)+f\{T(X_i)\}\right]
$$

Examples:

\begin{align*}
T(X)&=1-X,& X&\sim\Unif[0,1]^d,\\
T(X)&=-X,& X&\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mSigma)
\end{align*}

Although $X_i$ and $T(X_i)$ are dependent, the pairs are independent across $i$

The variance is

$$
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{Anti},n})
=\frac{\var\{f(X)\}}{2n}
\left[1+\corr\{f(X),f(T(X))\}\right]
$$

Antithetic sampling helps when the paired function values are [negatively correlated]{.alert}

## Constructing an antithetic variate {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

If $X$ has continuous CDF $F$, then

\begin{gather*}
U=F(X)\sim\Unif[0,1],\\
1-U\sim\Unif[0,1],\\
T(X)=F^{-1}\{1-F(X)\}\sim F
\end{gather*}

For a symmetric distribution, this often reduces to reflection about the center

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>For which monotone functions $f$ does $f(X)$ become negatively correlated with $f\{T(X)\}$?</span>
:::

## Latin hypercube sampling in one dimension {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="sampling"}

Place one independent uniform point in each of $n$ equal strata:

$$
X_i=\frac{i+U_i}{n},
\qquad U_i\ \IIDsim\ \Unif[0,1],
\qquad i=0,\ldots,n-1
$$

Then $X_i\sim\Unif[i/n,(i+1)/n]$ and

\begin{align*}
\Ex(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\Ex\{f(X_i)\}\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\int_{i/n}^{(i+1)/n}f(x)\,\dif x\\
&=\int_0^1f(x)\,\dif x
\end{align*}

The $X_i$ are independent but [not identically distributed]{.alert}

## One-dimensional LHS variance {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

Because the strata are independent,

$$
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\var\{f(X_i)\}
$$

For differentiable $f$, the mean value and Taylor theorems imply

\begin{align*}
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&\le\frac{\norm{f'}_\infty^2}{n^3},\\
\rmse(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&\le\frac{\norm{f'}_\infty}{n^{3/2}}
\end{align*}

In one dimension, stratification can improve the IID $n^{-1/2}$ RMSE rate to $n^{-3/2}$ for smooth $f$

## Latin hypercube sampling in $d$ dimensions {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="sampling"}

Let $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d$ be independent random permutations of $0,\ldots,n-1$:

$$
X_{i\ell}=\frac{\pi_\ell(i)+U_{i\ell}}n,
\qquad U_{i\ell}\ \IIDsim\ \Unif[0,1]
$$

Each coordinate uses every stratum exactly once

For $R$ independent Latin hypercubes,

\begin{align*}
\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)}
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(X_i^{(r)}),\\
\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R}
&=\frac1R\sum_{r=1}^R\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)},\\
\widehat{\var}(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R})
&=\frac1{R(R-1)}\sum_{r=1}^R
\left(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)}-\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R}\right)^2
\end{align*}

## Comparing random designs {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="sampling"}

Each design has $n=64$ points in $[0,1]^2$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "IID, Latin hypercube, and scrambled Sobol' point sets with 64 points in the unit square"
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 96%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import qmc

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"
n = 64
rng = np.random.default_rng(56504)
designs = {
    "IID": rng.random((n, 2)),
    "Latin hypercube": qmc.LatinHypercube(d=2, seed=56504).random(n),
    "Scrambled Sobol'": qmc.Sobol(d=2, scramble=True, seed=56504).random_base2(6),
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 4.2), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, (title, points) in zip(axes, designs.items()):
    ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], s=24, color="#1f5a91", alpha=0.9)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=17)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$x_1$", fontsize=18, math_fontfamily="stix")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$x_2$", fontsize=18, math_fontfamily="stix")
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=11)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.14)
plt.show()
```

## Strengths and limitations of LHS {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="sampling"}

### Strengths

- No importance density, control variate, or conditional expectation required
- Can converge faster than IID sampling
- Guarantees one point in every one-dimensional stratum

### Limitations

- The sample size is fixed when the design is constructed
- Accuracy assessment requires independent replications
- Too many replications can erase the efficiency gain
- The one-dimensional $n^{-3/2}$ RMSE guarantee does not extend automatically to $d>1$

## From LHS to quasi-Monte Carlo {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

[Low discrepancy sampling]{.alert}, or quasi-Monte Carlo, improves space filling beyond one-dimensional stratification

For nodes $x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}$ and target distribution $F$,

\begin{align*}
D^2(\{x_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1},F;K)
&=\int_{\mathcal X^2}K(x,x')\,\dif F(x)\,\dif F(x')\\
&\quad-\frac2n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\int_{\mathcal X}K(x,x_i)\,\dif F(x)\\
&\quad+\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}K(x_i,x_j)
\end{align*}

We usually take $\mathcal X=[0,1]^d$ and seek nodes with small discrepancy

## Three interpretations of discrepancy {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

For the uniform target on $[0,1]^d$, discrepancy is

- [worst-case error]{.alert}

  $$
  \left\lvert\int f(x)\,\dif x-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(x_i)\right\rvert
  \le D\norm{f}_{\mathcal H_K}
  $$

- [average-case root mean squared error]{.alert} for $f$ drawn from a Gaussian process with covariance kernel $K$
- [distance between the target distribution and the empirical distribution]{.alert}

The kernel specifies the function class and the distributional features being measured

## The van der Corput sequence {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Write a nonnegative integer in base $b$:

$$
i=(\cdots i_2i_1i_0)_b
$$

Reverse the digits across the radix point:

$$
\phi_b(i)=(0.i_0i_1i_2\cdots)_b
=\frac{i_0}b+\frac{i_1}{b^2}+\frac{i_2}{b^3}+\cdots
$$

- Usually $b$ is prime; $b=2$ is common
- $\{\phi_b(i)\}_{i=0}^{b^m-1}$ contains the same points as $\{i/b^m\}_{i=0}^{b^m-1}$ in a different order
- Earlier points keep their order as the sample grows

::: {.key-point}
The van der Corput construction turns a fixed-size grid into an [extensible sequence]{.alert}
:::

## Four low discrepancy families {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

For $i=0,1,\ldots$:

| Family | Construction | Typical preferred size |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Kronecker | $x_i=i\vzeta\bmod1$ | none |
| Lattice | $x_i=\phi_b(i)\vzeta\bmod1$ | $n=b^m$ |
| Halton | $x_i=\{\phi_2(i),\phi_3(i),\phi_5(i),\ldots\}$ | none |
| Digital | $x_i=i_0c_0\oplus i_1c_1\oplus\cdots$ | $n=b^m$ |

Here $\oplus$ denotes digitwise addition modulo $b$

Different families balance [extensibility]{.alert}, [projection quality]{.alert}, and [fast construction]{.alert}

## Component-by-component construction {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Generators for lattice rules and digital nets may be chosen by number theory or computer search

The component-by-component strategy:

1. Choose a one-dimensional generator that minimizes a discrepancy criterion over relevant sample sizes
2. Freeze the first $\ell$ components
3. Search for component $\ell+1$ that minimizes discrepancy
4. Increase $\ell$ and repeat until $\ell=d$

::: {.key-point}
A high-dimensional design is built by [optimizing one coordinate at a time]{.alert}
:::

## Randomized low discrepancy sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Randomization aims for

$$
X_{\mathrm{rand},i}\sim\Unif[0,1]^d
$$

for every $i$, while preserving low discrepancy jointly

- [Random shift]{.alert}: $X_{\mathrm{rand},i}=x_i+\vDelta\bmod1$, especially for lattices and Kronecker sequences
- [Random digital shift]{.alert}: $X_{\mathrm{rand},i}=x_i\oplus\vDelta$, especially for digital sequences
- [Linear matrix or nested uniform scrambling]{.alert}, especially for digital sequences

Independent randomizations provide replications without reverting to IID point placement

## Why randomize? {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="stat-estim"}

- The estimator

  $$
  \hmu_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(X_{\mathrm{rand},i})
  $$

  is unbiased for $\Ex[f(X)]$, $X\sim\Unif[0,1]^d$
- Randomized nodes almost surely avoid the boundary, so Gaussian quantile transforms remain finite
- Independent randomizations allow variance and error estimation
- For smooth integrands, scrambled digital sequences can attain nearly $\Order(n^{-3/2})$ RMSE

Randomization combines [QMC space filling]{.alert} with [Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification]{.alert}

## Stopping criteria {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

Two practical questions are

\begin{align*}
\abs{\mu-\hmu_n}&\le\text{what?}\\
\abs{\mu-\hmu_n}&\le\varepsilon
\quad\text{for what $n$?}
\end{align*}

We want answers based only on the computed data $f(x_0),f(x_1),\ldots$

- IID sampling: use a Central Limit Theorem interval when justified
- Randomized low discrepancy sampling: use independent replications
- Deterministic low discrepancy sampling: possible criteria include
  - decay of estimated Fourier coefficients
  - Bayesian credible intervals based on a kernel model

::: {.key-point}
An efficient method needs both [fast error decay]{.alert} and a [reliable stopping rule]{.alert}
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder" .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="prob-stat-est"}

- Equivalent expectations can have dramatically different computational variance
- Exact transport chooses a map that makes the target-to-proposal correction
  constant; importance sampling retains the correction as unequal weights
- Importance proposals may be tailored to a particular integrand, while
  transported target samples can be reused for many integrands
- Control variates and conditioning remove variability using known structure
- Antithetic sampling and Latin hypercubes introduce useful dependence deliberately
- Low discrepancy sequences replace random clustering with balanced space filling
- Randomization restores unbiasedness and supports error estimation while retaining QMC efficiency
